paragraph.text: A5. "Animals aren't conscious and don't feel pain like we do"

the claim that animals aren't conscious isn't a neutral position in the face of the evidence: it contradicts the current scientific consensus. And the milder version, "they don't feel like we do", changes the subject: difference isn't absence, and in some respects their experience may be worse, because they don't understand what's happening and can't be reassured.
"Animals don't feel like we do; it's just reflex."
The serious version isn't Cartesian; it's neuroscientific. It was defended, for example, by Brian Key (2016) regarding fish:
Conscious pain, unlike nociception, depends on specific brain structures, such as the neocortex and its connections.
So these animals can react to harmful stimuli without any conscious experience of pain.
There's only moral harm when there's conscious experience.
So using them causes no moral harm.
(detecting a harmful stimulus, which can be automatic) and
(the unpleasant experience) is legitimate and important. The argument errs in assuming the first happens without the second in every species without a neocortex.
, more common in conversation: "they do feel, but not like us". This version doesn't deny sentience; it uses the difference to reduce the moral weight of suffering, without saying by how much or why.
fails at P1, which confuses a specific structure with the function it performs, and at P2, which ignores analogous structures in other animal groups.
"It's just reflex, like when the doctor taps your knee."
"They have no idea what's happening, so they don't suffer."
"Chickens don't even have the brains for that."
"Fish don't have a neocortex, so they don't feel pain."
"Do you really think a cow suffers the way a person does?"
"Nociception isn't pain; without the right cortical structures, there's no conscious experience."
"They feel, but not like us." (uses the difference to reduce the weight, without saying by how much)

When you accidentally step on a dog's tail, it yelps, moves away and is then afraid to come close. That isn't just the body moving by itself: it felt it, remembered it and became afraid. Scientists have studied this a lot, and today most agree that animals feel pain, fear and joy. It may be a little different from how we feel, but it hurts all the same.

This isn't an open question. In 2012, a group of neuroscientists signed the Cambridge Declaration stating that lacking a neocortex doesn't stop an animal from having affective experiences, and in 2024 the New York Declaration, signed by hundreds of researchers, went in the same direction. Saying "they don't feel like us" doesn't help either: different isn't less. A pig in the slaughterhouse doesn't understand what's happening and can't be reassured, which may make the experience worse, not better.
"If they don't feel, why does the pharmaceutical industry test painkillers on them?"
The argument has two very different versions, and they shouldn't be mixed up.
There's no conscious experience, only nociception
It's an empirical claim, and current evidence goes against it
They feel, but differently and less intensely
May be partly true, but doesn't authorize the conclusion; difference isn't absence
The strong version makes a known mistake in comparative neuroscience: confusing
. Requiring a neocortex for experience is like requiring bat wings for an animal to fly. Birds and octopuses, for example, solve complex problems with brain architectures very different from ours.

text.bold: 1. The scientific consensus is the opposite.

paragraph.text: The Cambridge Declaration (2012) states that "the absence of a neocortex does not appear to preclude an organism from experiencing affective states" and that non-human animals, "including all mammals and birds, and many other creatures, including octopuses", possess the neurological substrates that generate consciousness. The New York Declaration (2024) reaffirms the point and extends it: there's strong support for mammals and birds, and a "realistic possibility" of conscious experience in all vertebrates and many invertebrates.

text.bold: 2. Science doesn't rely on a single anatomical criterion.

paragraph.text: Pain assessment uses converging criteria: presence of nociceptors, opioid systems, behavior change after injury, learning to avoid what hurts, willingness to pay costs to avoid pain, the effect of painkillers on behavior (Sneddon et al., 2014). Fish, birds, mammals, octopuses and crabs pass several of these criteria.

text.bold: 3. Tests of emotional state are already routine in research.

paragraph.text: The judgment bias test, created by Harding, Paul and Mendl (2004), showed that rats in worse conditions interpret ambiguous signals more "pessimistically", as humans do in negative moods. The technique was later applied to many species. This isn't activist intuition: it's methodology published in top journals.

text.bold: 4. The law has already followed the evidence.

paragraph.text: A review of more than 300 studies, commissioned from Jonathan Birch's group (2021), concluded that cephalopods and decapods should be treated as sentient. The United Kingdom changed its law to recognize octopuses, lobsters and crabs as sentient beings.

An animal that doesn't understand what's happening can't prepare, can't be reassured, doesn't know the pain will pass and can't ask for help. In humans, the inability to understand and anticipate usually increases suffering, not reduces it. So the cognitive difference doesn't justify discounting the weight of suffering; in many cases it justifies increasing it.
"The absence of a neocortex does not appear to preclude an organism from experiencing affective states"; mammals, birds and octopuses possess the neurological substrates of consciousness
High as a synthesis of experts
Strong support for conscious experience in mammals and birds; a realistic possibility in all vertebrates and in cephalopods, decapods and insects
High as a synthesis of experts
A review of more than 300 studies concludes that cephalopods and decapods should be treated as sentient; the basis for the change in British law

(d) The strongest counter-reply: the hard problem of consciousness

The honest reply isn't "animals are machines", but: no one can explain why subjective experience exists, nor measure consciousness directly. Any behavior could, in principle, occur without anyone feeling. So attributing suffering to animals would be an inference by analogy, weaker the more distant the species. This is a legitimate philosophical concern, and the book doesn't pretend it doesn't exist.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: The same doubt applies to other humans.

paragraph.text: There's no direct measure of consciousness in anyone. If uncertainty were enough to ignore suffering, the same would hold for anyone who isn't me.
"We aren't sure" doesn't imply "they don't feel". It implies we must decide under uncertainty, which is different.

text.bold: Under uncertainty, the cost of error decides.

paragraph.text: Treating as sentient an animal that may not feel costs a different meal. Treating as insensible an animal that feels costs real suffering, multiplied by tens of billions of individuals a year. The New York Declaration states the same principle: when there's a realistic possibility of conscious experience, it's irresponsible to ignore it.

text.bold: The analogy isn't weak for farmed vertebrates.

paragraph.text: Pigs, cows, chickens and fish have nociceptors, opioid systems, physiological stress responses and avoidance behavior. The evolutionary distance is large for an insect, not for a mammal raised for food.

text.bold: The skeptic already acts as if they knew.

paragraph.text: Those who doubt animal pain accept anesthesia for their own dog before surgery, and accept that painkillers are tested on animals before reaching pharmacies.

text.bold: Uses the argument only for the animals they eat.

paragraph.text: Doubt about sentience rarely reaches dogs and cats.
Knowing an animal will be eaten reduces the mind we attribute to it
Classifying an animal as food reduces the perception that it suffers
Much stronger evidence is demanded for the uncomfortable conclusion
Fear of seeming naive leads to denying obvious similarities, the mirror error of anthropomorphizing
The suffering happens far away, with no sound or image for the consumer
The empirical basis of argument E7 ("I don't want to see")
Accepting sentience would require changing habits, so the doubt is kept
The principle being tested is: "whoever lacks the brain structures we have, or doesn't feel like us, can be disregarded".
Their pain could be ignored. A baby's cortex is still immature, and they neither report nor understand their own pain; by the criterion, there'd be no experience to protect
This belief underpinned surgery on babies with minimal anesthesia until the 1980s (Anand and Hickey, 1987)
They'd lose protection from pain. If experience depends exclusively on the cortex, patients with extensive cortical damage wouldn't suffer
Medicine treats these patients' pain, and there's evidence that subcortical structures are enough for basic affective states
Anyone could be treated as an automaton. There's no direct access to anyone's mind; other people's pain is always an inference
This is the old problem of other minds, and no one applies it to their own family
An extraterrestrial life form without neurons like ours could be tortured even if it showed every sign of suffering
Shows that the relevant criterion is functional evidence of experience, not anatomical similarity
Running it over or operating without anesthesia would be a matter of indifference. If animal pain is just reflex, that holds for all animals, not just the ones on the plate
Almost no one accepts this consequence, which shows the doubt is selective

The distinction between nociception and pain is real and important: not every reaction to a harmful stimulus involves conscious experience, and a plant closing its leaves isn't suffering. Caution against projecting human feelings onto anything that moves is also healthy. And there are real differences between species: a fish's experience is probably not the same as a pig's, nor a pig's the same as ours. About more distant invertebrates, such as insects, scientific uncertainty is still large, and the book doesn't pretend otherwise.

The mistake lies in turning difference into absence and uncertainty into license. The moral question isn't whether the animal feels exactly as we do, but whether there's someone there for whom it is bad. For the animals we raise and kill in the greatest numbers, the evidence that there is someone is strong.
